o: It registers a method as a consumer run by a listener container
It sends a message to Kafka when the method returns
It creates the Kafka topic automatically in production
It turns a REST endpoint into a message handler
questions.w: The container polls the broker, deserialises records and calls the method. Concurrency, error handling and offset commits are configured on the container.

questions.q: Two instances of a service use the same Kafka consumer group id. How are messages delivered?
o: Each partition is read by only one instance at a time
Both instances receive every message
Only the first instance receives any messages
Messages are split between instances by size
questions.w: More consumers than partitions leaves some idle. Use a different group id to give another service its own copy of the stream.

questions.q: A consumer processes a message and crashes before committing the offset. What happens on restart?
o: The message is delivered again, so processing must be idempotent
The message is lost for good and nobody notices
Kafka deletes the whole topic that held the message
The message arrives exactly once with no extra work needed
questions.w: This is at-least-once delivery. Record processed ids or use naturally idempotent operations.

questions.q: A poison message keeps failing. Which Spring Kafka setup avoids blocking the partition?
o: A `DefaultErrorHandler` with limited retries and a dead-letter topic
Retry for ever inside the very same listener thread
Ignore every exception that the listener might throw
Commit the offsets before the message is processed
questions.w: After the retries the record goes to `<topic>.DLT` so the consumer moves on and the failure can be inspected and replayed.

questions.q: Why does a Kafka consumer's `max.poll.interval.ms` matter for slow processing?
o: If handling takes longer, the broker assumes the consumer died and rebalances
It sets the maximum size of any single message on the topic
It controls how many records a producer sends in a batch
It encrypts the connection between the consumer and the broker
questions.w: A rebalance moves its partitions to another consumer, which can cause duplicates. Process fast, or hand work to other threads carefully.

questions.q: What is a safe way to publish an event after saving to the database?
o: The transactional outbox, saving the event in the same transaction
Publish first and save the data in the database afterwards
Publish inside a loop until the broker finally answers
Skip the database entirely and only publish the event
questions.w: Publishing directly can leave the database and broker disagreeing after a crash. The outbox relay publishes committed events.

questions.q: What is Spring Cloud Stream for?
o: Broker-agnostic producers and consumers written as functional beans
Streaming live video from a server to many browsers
Generating typed REST clients from OpenAPI specs
Compiling Kotlin code into a native executable
questions.w: You write `Consumer<T>`, `Function<T,R>` or `Supplier<T>` beans. Binders connect them to Kafka or RabbitMQ.

questions.q: What does consumer lag tell you?
o: How far behind the latest offset the consumer group is
How many consumers currently exist in the group
How large the messages in the partition are
How many topics the broker is currently serving
questions.w: Rising lag means consumers cannot keep up. It is a key alert metric. Scale consumers (up to the partition count) or speed up processing.
